DR HUW MAYBERRY (recalled) (via video link)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Members of the jury, you'll note that Dr Mayberry is on screen.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Good evening, Dr Mayberry. Can you hear me? We couldn't hear your reply, Dr Mayberry. We saw your lips move. Try again. Can you hear me?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And I can hear you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Good.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry, when you last gave evidence you told us about your responsibilities in relation to the baby [Baby O] on a night shift that began on 22 June 2016. Today, we'd like to
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: ask you questions in relation to his brother, [Baby P] or [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is it right that your next shift at the hospital was for a night shift that began on 23 June 2016?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We know from evidence that between those shifts, sadly, [Baby O] died. Were you aware of that fact before your shift began or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was made aware of it during a discussion with one of my colleagues, Dr Jessica Burke, who'd informed me about what had happened.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Was that a discussion within the workplace as part of the handover or was that a discussion elsewhere?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was inside the workplace. Both the paediatric and the neonatal handover occur in one of the rooms in the paediatric ward and it was there where I had the discussion with Dr Burke.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Was, in effect, Dr Burke handing over her responsibilities to you and updating you on relevant developments?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was before the main part of the handover. I think Jess had wanted me to know before proceeding with the main part of the handover.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I understand. As part of the handover proper, were you informed of any changes in the planned management of [Baby O]'s brothers, [Baby P] and [Baby R]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So Jess had told me that the other two patients, [Baby P] and [Baby R], had been reviewed by Dr Gibbs and he had started -- he'd done a septic screen or initiated a septic screen on the children because of the concerns about the deterioration of [Baby O] and had reviewed them not long before evening handover.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Could you just remind us of the timetabled time for that doctors' handover as opposed a nurses' handover. What does time the medics' night shift again?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember the exact times at the Countess of Chester. I think it was -- it was between 8 and 9 o'clock, but I think it was normally around 8.30 to the best of my recollection.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. I wonder, Mr Murphy, could you put up tile 134, please? If we could look at the original note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Just to set everyone's minds at rest.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There was a fault in the system, there was no fire alarm, no proper fire alarm, so don't be concerned that we should be evacuating, we shouldn't.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry, can you see the clinical note on screen?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll see that it was timed at 18.00 hours, signed off by Dr Burke. It begins with the words:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Reviewed -- Dr Gibbs."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It would seem from the chronology that you provided to us that this was the review of [Baby P] and indeed [Baby R] made by Dr Gibbs shortly after [Baby O]'s sad demise.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Having re-read that note, does that accord with the verbal appraisal that you received from your colleague, Dr Burke?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: It would seem that the baby had been tolerating nasogastric tube feeds and there was a plan put in place. In short, is the first point of that plan to take bloods from the baby and to screen those samples for full results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: The second part of the plan, is that the introduction of antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Was it your understanding that this was a precautionary measure, made because of [Baby O]'s unexpected demise?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So normally, at the time -- if you're worried about sepsis in twins, or triplets in this case, if one of them became unwell, then you would initiate a septic screen on the remaining children.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Is that effectively an established and widely embraced protocol in relation to all multiple pregnancy children?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it was at the time, although I've sort of moved out of this area of paediatrics subsequent to this.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm sure it's not controversial. I think your statement suggests that it was actually part of national guidance in this regard.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, I believe it was at the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm grateful. In any event, they were the steps and they were the reasons behind those steps taken in relation to [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In addition to that, were you informed that there was to be an adjustment in the feeding regime for [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the initial discussion was that [Baby P] would continue having nasogastric feeds, but if there were to be any concern overnight, then the feeds should be stopped and fluids should be started -- sorry, intravenous fluids.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Were you appraised of any decision-making as to the quantity of feeds to be continued for [Baby P] at that point or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall, sorry.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Very well. So having been told of the change of management plan and the fact that Dr Gibbs was steering this course as a precautionary measure, did you attend upon [Baby P] or did you go about other business at that point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I initially had a phone discussion with one of the nursing staff who had told me that they'd had some higher volumes of aspirates from the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So normally, before they gave more milk down the nasogastric tube, they aspirated the tube to see how much feed remained in the stomach. They told me that they were having a few millilitres of aspirate, and at that point I, out of an abundance of caution, made a decision that the best thing to do would be to go to the neonatal unit and see how things proceeded, how [Baby P] was.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: On arrival at the neonatal unit, just after I had walked through the doors, the emergency bleep went off with a call to, I think it was A&E resus, and so at that point I had to immediately go and attend to another child who was in an emergency condition.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: At that point I had to make a decision and while normally having aspirates from a nasogastric tube on a child that you're feeding is not by any means an unusual step to see, I thought the safest plan would be to ask the nursing staff to move [Baby P] on to IV fluids.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Could I invite you to break that down and assist us as to when these events occurred? From memory, approximately how far into your shift were you when you had that telephone conversation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This was straight after evening handover to the best of my recollection.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So approximately what time of night?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'd have thought about 9.30.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Can you remember who initiated that communication, you or your nursing colleague?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe it was my nursing colleague.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Do you remember how they caught your attention?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think they had given -- to the best of my recollection, it was a normal bleep that they had bleeped me on.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: To which you responded, I take it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And at that point I made the decision to go the unit.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I know it's a lot to ask, but can you remember the identity of the nursing colleague you spoke to at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think it was Belinda Simcock to the best of my recollection.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: The report you received, you've just told us, was to the effect that there'd been a small amount of aspirate withdrawn from [Baby P]'s digestive system; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Are you able to help as to quantity with any more precision?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe the phrase that was used was that [Baby P] was having some increased aspirates from his nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Were you informed of the nature of the aspirates, whether they were milky, bilious or what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was told that they were milky.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. The withdrawal of a milky aspirate from the system of a neonate, in isolation would that be a matter of particular concern or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not in isolation, no.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: What are the potential causes of a failure to fully digest a feed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There are many causes. For a lot of children it can be normal and it's part of having reduced movement through their gut of feed. Some children may have reduced movement of milk through their gut for other reasons, so if you're worried about them having an infection or having something like necrotising enterocolitis -- however, to the best of my knowledge, and this is probably something that I've gained more knowledge about following -- in subsequent years, nobody really knows what a large volume, as it were, of aspirate is, and practice varies across the United Kingdom as to how often people check aspirates, when people check aspirates and what people would do about large levels of aspirates.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. I wonder whether we could take down the note from the screen so we can see Dr Mayberry again.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Apologies for that, Dr Mayberry, my oversight.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No problem.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So to summarise the answer you just gave, in isolation ordinarily this might not be a matter of concern, but of course we know that you knew that [Baby P]'s brother [Baby O] had died in the very recent past.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Did that fact operate on your mind when deciding how to respond to this telephone call?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, because I was worried about how [Baby O] had deteriorated and, not having an adequate answer at the time for the reason why he had deteriorated, I felt the best course of action to do was to stop feeds at the time and put him on IV fluids. I had a very low threshold in my mind to do that.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: A very low threshold and was that an adjusted -downwards adjusted threshold because of [Baby O]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So your management advice was to withdraw all nasogastric feeds and to place [Baby P] on a regime of, the notes suggest, 10% dextrose intravenously; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Just to recap on your evidence, you were telling us how you went to the neonatal unit to effect this plan; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: But however, before you actually got to [Baby P]'s cot side, there was an emergency elsewhere that caused you to go back from where you came from, effectively?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Did you return to the neonatal unit during the course of that shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall if I returned just before evening handover -- before morning handover for that shift.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I may have done. I certainly do recall at one point, at about 4 o'clock in the morning, I rang the neonatal unit from the resus department in accident and emergency, where I was dealing with another sick child, because I hadn't heard back if there had been any further progress with [Baby P]. I was informed that he was doing well and that there were no concerns from the nursing staff about his condition at that point.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. So to piece the chronology together, you'd gone to the NNU intending to attend upon [Baby P], an emergency caused you to go to the A&E resus, and did that emergency keep you there for several hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You next communicated in relation to [Baby P] at about 4 am, when you made a phone call to check on his progress?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: What information did you receive during that second [Baby P]-related telephone call?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He said, "I was informed he was doing well and there were no concerns".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: No need to go over it again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Was there anything in particular, Dr Mayberry, that you might assist us with in relation to his nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you mind... I'm sorry, do you mind clarifying that a little more, sorry?
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Certainly. Your statement, and I am sure this is not controversial, suggests that you were informed, and you directed, that his nasogastric tube should be left on free drainage. Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And the purpose of that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The purpose of that would be to drain off any fluids or air within his tummy, which might be accumulating.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. So having been so appraised by a telephone call, were you assured and satisfied with the continuing management of [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Did you hand over responsibility to medical colleagues at the end of your shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And do you recall that? Do you recall who you spoke to and what, if anything, in particular, you suggested?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I will have to refer to my statement, sorry. I believe I spoke to the consultant who was on during the day and the medical registrar who was on during the day to inform them --
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Again, I'm sure it's uncontroversial. Your statement suggests you spoke to Dr Gibbs directly and asked him to see [Baby P] as a first priority. Does that --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: -- accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Does that conclude your involvement with any of the [Surname of Babies O, P & R] triplets?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Could you remain there and answer any questions asked of you?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Mayberry, you've explained to us that there was a particular concern to monitor [Baby P] closely because of what had happened with [Baby O]; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: In fact, on the night shift that you were working, you were contacted about [Baby P], weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I've said previously, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You did set off to go to examine him in the neonatal unit, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: But you never actually examined him at all, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: What you're telling us about him is based upon telephone calls, maybe two or so telephone calls, with nursing staff, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And you never got as far as being able to make any clinical notes in the records for [Baby P], did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And the reason for that is that you were called away because you were required in a different part of the hospital, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Which, as it happens, is the same reason that you'd been unable to make the note with regard to [Baby O] the night before, although you had actually seen [Baby O]; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You can't give us any first-hand knowledge as a doctor of how [Baby P] was presenting that night, can you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, apart from -- not first-hand knowledge, no.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: The first thing that was brought to your attention, you tell us, is a telephone call from one of the nurses to -- was that to tell you that [Baby P] had produced a few millilitres of milk; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A few millilitres of milk had been aspirated from his nasogastric tube, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. So there's a phone call of a few millilitres of milk aspirated from his NGT. Your recollection, Dr Mayberry, is that you received that phone call not long after the handover that had taken place; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So you think maybe round about 9.30 in the evening, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You also say that you recall it was Belinda Simcock.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There may not be much that turns on this but just as a matter of record, it may be Belinda Simcock was not actually working that evening. Might it have been Kate Percival-Ward, as she was, or Sophie Ellis, who contacted you, or is it just too difficult after this period of time to be sure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My recollection was of Belinda Simcock, but if she was not working that evening then obviously that's an incorrect recollection.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: All right. We can check that. I don't anticipate anyone would expect you to recall precisely who now.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's not a criticism: some time has gone by.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A few millilitres of milk being aspirated from an NGT may not be a concern; is that your opinion, Dr Mayberry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think... It's my opinion now that having aspirates from an NGT would be considered, in many cases, normal.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: When you say "a few millilitres", what figure did you understand "a few millilitres" to be?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't recall at the time what my opinion of what a few millilitres was at that time.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: But to assist us in any event with this, as you sit there now, what do you consider "a few millilitres" to be, what quantity of millilitres?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Five, 10ml.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And if the quantity becomes larger, depending on how large it is, is that likely to be more of a concern?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At the time I would have said yes. And now I would have said it's not possible to say.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: In any event, when you say a few millilitres you say up to -- did you say up to 5 or 10ml, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I believe so, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: All right. I just want to show you a feeding chart that we have. It's tile 24. This should come on your screen. We'll just open it up so you can see it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to enlarge the readings we have in the lower righthand corner. We have the timings and I can tell you what the timings are when we go there, Dr Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sure.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: It's difficult to see so I'm going to ask if we can enlarge the top -- the bolder entries to the right-hand side, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: First of all, can you see the third column from the right with writing has got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "DEBM NGT 15. 136. 14ml R."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that, Dr Mayberry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "DEBM NGT 15ml" -- and what was, sorry, the other thing that you were asking about?
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm just checking. Below that it says "136". The cursor is on the screen there. And below that it says "14ml"; do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We know that is an entry for 8 pm, for 20.00 hours, on that evening. The next entry that you can see to the right of that, where we have the running total below DEBM of 151, the cursor is there, that is at 22.00 hours. Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Then the final entry on the right-hand side at 00.00 hours is for 20ml that was aspirated. Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: First of all, from what you tell us, is it right that you didn't know about the 14ml that had been aspirated at 20.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would have been, to the best of my recollection, before my handover and I don't recall being handed over the 14ml of aspirate.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You mean you don't recall being told about that at the time of handover?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: The 20ml to the right-hand side, once that aspirate had been produced -- obtained, [Baby P] was made nil by mouth.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You can see it says "stopped" on the total column.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: That happened at midnight, not 21.30.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: But whatever your recollection, do you agree 20ml is a substantial quantity of milk to have been aspirated from [Baby P]'s NGT?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. It's a reasonable amount of milk to aspirate.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: It's significantly more than the figure you give us as what you believed a few millilitres to be, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: But from what you tell us, you never realised that in fact it was 20ml that had been aspirated at that time; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And do you agree that 14ml being aspirated at 20.00, followed by a further 20ml aspirated at midnight, may be a cause for concern?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a... It's a difficult question to answer. There's many things to take into account as opposed to looking at a single number of aspirates in that chart on its own. The chart says that the child is opening their bowels and passing meconium, which would suggest that they're having ongoing gut transit. So aspirating 14ml in that context is slightly offset by the fact, you know, the child is opening their bowels.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So on its own as a number, yes, it's a reasonable amount, but there is enough during the day to suggest that this child is moving -- their gut is moving and therefore a suggestion that their gut is healthy.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: But 14ml followed by 20ml may be something that is clinically significant in a bad way, mightn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In terms of an evidence base for knowing how much you can aspirate off somebody's nasogastric tube in relation to their feeds and what that means, there isn't a very good evidence base for saying how well that correlates with disease in newborns and in children in acute and critical care.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You explained that as part of the plan on handover, it had been decided that if there were any concerns overnight [Baby P] would be made nil by mouth; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And [Baby P] was made nil by mouth, wasn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So it follows, doesn't it, that the aspirate that was reported to you was potentially a cause of concern?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was a cause of concern for myself as I mentioned earlier on, yes, because of what had happened with [Baby O] and not knowing why he had deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: At the time he was made nil by mouth, you had no idea of the actual volume of the aspirate, did you, accurate idea?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did not, no.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Can I just ask you something that follows that and I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up tile 237, please. This is a continuation of that chart into the early hours of the morning, Dr Mayberry, so you can understand what we're looking at.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You can see there the chart as it carries on and I'm just going to look briefly at the entries under "output" towards the bottom of the chart, a couple of entries in particular. If you look where it says -- under the word "output", you have the line for aspirates and if you look four columns along you'll come to -it says "25ml air".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So you told us Dr Ukoh was there round about 9.30.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have told us that [Dr A] was around, I think you put it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Do you remember any other doctors during the course of the day coming to assist?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Brearey. He would have done an echocardiograph. And I know [Dr B] was liaising with the tertiary unit.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was trying to secure a transfer for him to go to a tertiary unit. The tertiary unit consultant made his way over, Dr Rackham.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: We're going to hear that he arrived about 3 o'clock if that assists you with timings.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Did the number of doctors present during the course of the day strike you at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was fortuitous that they were all around at the time because it was a case of all hands on deck and we could get as much expertise in where it was needed to try and help [Baby P]. But yeah, it was good that there was so many doctors around.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Do you recall any other nurses that were present during the course of the shift? We've been through the list.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Any involved --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yvonne Farmer was helping. We were having to draw up special drugs called inotropes to support [Baby P]'s blood pressure and that takes two people to draw up and administer. Yvonne was helping, helping us both drawing up medications.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: "Both" being you and Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Do you remember Rebecca Morgan, the student, assisting at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was involved in [Baby P]'s care at the beginning of the shift. Although I think, to be fair, she wasn't used to this sort of situation. I think she was quite overwhelmed and overcome --
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and became quite upset.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Do you recall during the course of the day the need for intraosseous needles having to be deployed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Exactly -- not exactly what time, no.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it's fair to say that with Dr Rackham being a neonatologist and an expert in his field, he did sort of orchestrate things and become like the team leader.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: I think it's fair to say he had expertise, you know, that perhaps our consultants didn't possess. And yes, he did become team leader.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Do you recall the course of the resuscitation after he arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Unfortunately, I'm fairly sure that was, sadly, the final collapse of [Baby P] shortly after Dr Rackham arrived.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: We've heard that that, tragically, was unsuccessful, that final resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Do you recall what you did after [Baby P] had passed away?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think we were all in a state of shock, but I think we had already brought [Baby O] in his cooled cot into the nursery so he could be with his brothers, with the parents' consent, obviously, so that they could be together before -- when it is known that it's futile, really, with [Baby P], that he wasn't going to make it, so we had [Baby O] in the nursery as well. So it was all about supporting the parents, which Lucy took charge of.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Your recollection is you brought [Baby O] into nursery 2?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, after I spoke with the parents, obviously. I only did it with their consent.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Of course. [Baby R] was still in nursery 2 at this point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, he was.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: How was [Baby R] towards the end of your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thankfully, he was incredibly stable. I think it's fair to say he was fine. He'd been put on triple antibiotics as a precaution. He was nil by mouth. He was on a drip. He was in his incubator and it was agreed that he would be taken to the tertiary unit.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Okay. What was the feeling about [Baby R] at that point, the two triplets having passed away so suddenly? Were there any concerns for [Baby R]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Fearful, yes. Really fearful. This is -- we thought it can't possibly happen again. You were just terrified it could happen again.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Did you notice anything about [Baby R] that caused you any concern?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He did have a slight distended abdomen, but nothing of any concern, it wasn't tense or loopy or discoloured, it was just a little bit distended, nothing more than that.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Is that something you'd noticed earlier in the shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.text: Thank you, Nurse Booth. I have no more questions, but if you could wait there, please.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Without a doubt, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOOTH

Witness statement of DR KATARZYNA COOKE (read)

My Lord, members of the jury, may I read two witness statements, please. The first is a statement made by Dr Katarzyna Cooke, dated 8 March 2018. The jury will recall the earlier evidence of Dr Cooke in which she informed us of her professional status within the Countess of Chester as of summer 2016 and her professional development since then.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So if I --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And your comment on the quality of her handwriting, shortly before --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Shortly before I couldn't read her handwriting, yes, quite so.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm trying to put it -- you'll remember Dr Cooke, I'm not being discourteous to her, but she spoke with an Eastern European accent.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She told us she was Polish and she remembered the Brexit referendum date.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If Mr Murphy could put up tile 64, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This is the 8 March 2018 statement?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could click on the note. I'm grateful. If I now read from the statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On Thursday, 23 June 2016, I remember that I was involved in the morning ward round and conducted a review of [Baby O] and
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby P]. The babies were two of a set of triplets, their brother being [Baby R].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The morning ward round is a routine process which is conducted every day, whereby we assess all the babies in the unit and decide a management plan. The nurses are kept up to date with any changes in the plan. They flag up any concerns re patients' handover from the previous shift or current ones."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, moving to page 7 of the reading bundle:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have reviewed the notes shown to me in relation to [Baby P], the brother of [Baby O]. [Baby P] was reviewed at 10.00 hours on 23 June 2016 during the ward round, approximately 30 minutes after I had conducted [Baby O]'s review.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From the notes, I can see that he was a good birth weight for a premature triplet. He had the same problems as [Baby O]: he was on CPAP due to apnoea and he had also been commenced on antibiotics as a routine precaution. The antibiotics were stopped and he was doing a little better than his brother as he was breathing unassisted in air.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby P] was establishing his feeds on donor milk and he had been tolerating them well. On examination, there were no remarks and a similar plan was implemented to that of [Baby O]: to continue establishing [Baby P]'s feeds and to complete baby checks along with a cranial ultrasound review when appropriate.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have documented that [Baby P]'s abdomen appeared full, but this is also subject to whether a baby has just had a feed, therefore we are required to look at the bigger clinical picture. His observations were normal and there were no concerns. [Baby P] was breathing unassisted with no sign of respiratory distress, which is really good for a baby of his gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "He had active bowel sounds and no aspirates and I would describe him as a well baby at that time."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If I could ask Mr Murphy to move to tile 134, please. Returning to Dr Cooke's statement, she states:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs was the on-call consultant that evening and conducted a thorough review of him [[Baby P]] and I was completing the writing for him. It doesn't seem like there were any concerns or any dynamic changes from the review in the morning. Dr Gibbs did decide to commence [Baby P] on antibiotics and he requested an abdominal X-ray as a precaution and to rule out NEC.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The next entry I have documented is at 18.00 hours, which is way beyond the time when everything had happened that day with [Baby O]. I am aware that Dr Gibbs reviewed the surviving triplets post-[Baby O]'s collapse. I later documented in the notes that [Baby P] is stable and continuing to breathe unassisted, tolerating his feeds well, and is active upon handling.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs notes that [Baby P] had a normal breathing pattern and his abdomen is full, mildly distended but without tenderness, and active bowel sounds. [Baby P] appeared to have redness at the base of his umbilicus. This may have been due to scratching caused by his nappy or cord clamp. This could have been a genuine concern but it is unlikely in a well baby. It is not an uncommon finding as the clamp on the umbilical cord is made from plastic and, when tucked inside the nappy, due to a premature baby's fragile skin, it could have caused scratching.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In cases of multiple pregnancy, whereby something has happened to one of the babies from a medical perspective we would have an extremely low threshold for review and very close monitoring of other siblings. Dr Gibbs also made the decision to do a full blood count along with bilirubin and started him on second-line routine antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In consideration of [Baby P]'s belly button and to cover every eventuality, [Baby P] was prescribed flucloxacillin, which was a standard treatment of a suspected infection within the umbilicus. It is also documented that an abdominal X-ray was requested. These actions are precautionary measures taken, especially in view of [Baby O]'s collapse. It is to anticipate the problems and be able to act on it early enough to avoid long-term issues.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The following day, Friday, 24 June 2016, I was working at the Countess of Chester Hospital and I was either on call again or holding the bleep for the neonatal senior house officer. I certainly recall working with the registrar, Tony Ukoh, as he was my senior that day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There is no record of my name on the medical notes for [Baby P], but I think I assisted with CPR on [Baby P] following his collapse. From what I can recall, [Baby P] experienced desaturation and bradycardia. This would not resolve, so we continued on to CPR. I think I was performing cardiac massage until a number of seniors entered the room and they took over. This recollection is from my memory alone.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The deaths of both triplets was the first time I had seen a neonatal death in my whole career and therefore it has left a lasting imprint on my memory. I would describe it as quite
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: striking. [Baby P]'s death was unexpected, especially as I do not recall any concerns raised by nursing staff, nor the night team of doctors on call. This recollection is from memory alone."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That concludes that aspect of Dr Cooke's evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She made another statement, which is at page 11, dated 18 May 2018, which states during the time she worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital she had some involvement with the care of a set of triplets born on 21 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She repeats that on Thursday, 23 June, whilst working at the Countess, she completed the morning ward round within the neonatal unit and, at approximately 09.30, she conducted a review of [Baby O]. I am looking at page 3 of 4 at 13. It is largely repetitious, but she states:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I conducted an examination of [Baby P] at approximately 10.00 hours during the morning ward round of 23 June 2016. This was about 30 minutes after my examination of [Baby O] but was 24 hours prior to [Baby P]'s collapse and subsequent death.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I complete the morning ward round, I review each baby in a very systematic manner. I review the nurses' observations, respiratory support, fluids and cardiovascular concerns. I then go through the medication prescribed to the baby and any concerns in relation to sepsis. I believe at the time, and considering my qualification grade of being a doctor, I did not miss anything and everything was correctly documented.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Now, due to my neonatal experience and having worked in this area a little longer, I know that if there was any acute problem or change, [Baby P] would not have presented in a normal, reassuring way. To my knowledge, there is nothing from either my recollection of memory or any notes that would concern me at that time in relation to the examination of either [that is to say [Baby O] or [Baby P]] baby."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, is that a convenient moment or would you like me to read the next statement?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I think if we just read the next statement, it'll only take a few minutes. We'll run slightly beyond 1 o'clock, but we'll still have the hour for lunch.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS YVONNE FARMER (read)
Yvonne Rose Farmer made a statement dated 3 March 2018 stating that she qualified as a nurse in April 1997 and in October 2000 she returned to the Countess of Chester Hospital
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: and stayed within the neonatal unit at this hospital until the present day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At page 16, my Lord. She asserts that:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am a band 6 nurse and I work clinically, but part of my job is referred to as practice development, but it is a role as an educator and concerns the development of the unit within guidelines, introducing new equipment and training our staff to use the equipment. I would describe being an educator as a role I have grown into."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At page 17, and if I could ask Mr Murphy, with my learned friend's agreement, to put up J23866, which is a nursing note which corresponds to the entry within the statement that I'm about to read:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 22 June 2016 I was working a long day clinical shift on the unit, which had commenced at 07.30 hours. I recall looking after [Baby P] on this date and I think I also looked after one other patient.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Halfway through my shift, [Baby P] was doing really well on CPAP, so we stepped him down on to high flow. Again, this is humidified gases, but it is a flow and the infant does most of the breathing. Respiratory-wise, [Baby P] seemed to be doing okay and we checked the gases once the respiratory support had been changed. These results appeared good and so he was left on this flow. [Baby P] started off on a flow of 5 litres and this was reduced to 4 litres at 16.00 hours that day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby P] was nil by mouth. Again, this is quite common as you are supporting the work of breathing and you don't want to compromise this by filling their stomach with milk. He was on intravenous fluids via a cannula line in his hand or foot. Again, this is the normal practice of administering intravenous fluids.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During this shift, we conducted hourly checks on the cannula site and I noticed that there was tissuing (the site was becoming blocked) and instead of the fluids travelling via the
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: vein, the vein breaks down and travels via the tissues.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "A cause of this is due to prematurity. As the vein is so narrow, it breaks down and causes local swelling, so the cannula is removed and a new one inserted into another vein, but there is no permanent damage caused. There are signs you look out for. Symptoms include redness, swelling or if the baby appears to be in any pain.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I had informed the doctor about the tissuing but, as we were busy at the time, no one could replace the cannula straightaway. As a result, I had been asked to start some feeds so they could reduce the amount of intravenous fluids.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the afternoon, one of the consultants sited a new line, recommenced intravenous fluids and continued with a small amount of feeds. Again, this is calculated on the weight of the baby to a ratio of millilitres per kilogram and [Baby P] was given 75ml per kilogram. [Baby P]'s cannula was later changed and he was showing signs of toleration with no vomiting and his stomach was not distended, so we were happy to continue with the feeds.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER
