blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So what did do you then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: We then proceeded -- at this point [Dr A] had also come. So this now becomes more than one people (sic).
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So one person is looking after the airway --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I am going to interrupt you again, I am sorry. Do we take it from what you have said [Dr A] wasn't there to start with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: He wasn't there to start with but then he arrived and took over the airway management over from Dr Ukoh. He put the Guedel airway in and started bagging and we were getting ready for intubation. Around this time the adrenaline was also given, the IV access is lost, and Dr Ukoh and I moved to this end to start --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Someone is taking a note of what you say, so I'm going to ask you to slow down. Lots going on at once.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Dr A] has taken over the airway?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He's introduced a Guedel airway, which we've heard about before?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Preparations are being made for intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And in the meantime, drugs are being administered, initially via an intravenous line, but then that line is lost; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So in the first instance, both Dr Ukoh and I attempted to re-site an intravenous line, which is through -- which is inserting a cannula. I do not recall how many attempts, but normally in a very sick baby or a child, we would not spend too long before moving to an intraosseous route, keeping in mind then when a baby collapses circulation is very poor and obtaining intravenous access can be very challenging. However,
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: it is very important to have some kind of an access and an alternative to intravenous access is intraosseous access.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have heard that's through the bone in the leg, into the bone marrow within.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And that enables intravenous drugs --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Intraosseous, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, intraosseous as it then becomes. Can we return to your note so you don't have to try to remember too much because I think you have made a note as to what unfolded with the intraosseous access. If we can go down, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have then noted:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Airway maintained with Neopuff whilst bagged whilst getting intubation ready. Few attempts at IV access unsuccessful. [Dr A] arrived and took over airway from Dr Ukoh. Dr Ukoh and I inserted an intraosseous, [is that] needle"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "First in left (Dr Ukoh)..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that his action?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... and then the right (by myself)."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Heart rate falling."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then you put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Adrenaline was given via intraosseous access."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Intubated successfully at first attempt by [Dr A]."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So scroll down a little further, please. You have then put that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Dr A] and I were present with [Baby P] through the day. For detailed notes on management and resuscitation, please refer to [Dr A]'s note entries."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that presumably is for times and quantities and the like?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Whilst the drugs are being delivered via the intraosseous route, did resuscitation continue?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So again, I have not made detailed notes here, but with the -- I think he had at least four collapses.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He had three or four doses of adrenaline and a sodium chloride bolus before the return of spontaneous circulation --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, again, if it assists you, it was not too long after 10 o'clock that [Dr A] notes that [Baby P] stabilised.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Once that first collapse or the emergency had passed of that first collapse, did you then go to contact somebody else?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So as I've written here as well, after this happened, this was now beginning to really concern me, that it was very similar to what had happened the day before. We had stabilised [Baby P] and I went away to speak to the neonatal transport team consultant, Dr Rackham, who is the same -- so it can be a different person, but it happened to be Dr Rackham who had been the same consultant that I'd spoken to the previous day for [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was intravenous access, [Baby P] now -- the emergency having passed for now, was intravenous access regained?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So again there is a detailed note of that in my notes. I'll just clarify here, basically, very shortly after [Baby P]'s passing, [Dr A] and I sat down and discussed the chronology of events and when -- what happened and just to make some sense of what had happened and I wrote my statement with
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: times and what had actually happened in my statement very shortly after. So in that, I have made a note that once [Baby P] was stable, [Dr A] managed to site an IV access. I think one was on the right side and a short while later on the left. So not long after the first resuscitation, he had a -- one intravenous access and then, after that, two intravenous accesses, plus an intraosseous access.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When babies, or even older children, are unwell, it is recommended that they have at least two intravenous accesses, one, because multiple medication can be needed, and two, you have a back-up in case one stops working.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Shall we return to your note, then, if we may?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you've made a note that you spoke to Dr Rackham at about 10.30 and updated him about [Baby P], you were advised that they would enquire whether a bed was available and also to try to take [Baby R] to the same unit was the plan. That was the parents' request so that they could be together; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You then go on to talk about speaking to Dr Rackham at 1 pm, but picking up about what you were saying about the times and sitting down with [Dr A], [Dr A] has recorded another desaturation and bradycardia at 11.30, involving [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And a serious one; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you have a recollection of that second collapse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, I do. The second collapse, again, the oxygen saturation dropped and the heart rate dropped and he needed full resuscitation with adrenaline, bicarbonate and sodium chloride boluses.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Which we've heard are the standard resuscitation drugs in these circumstances?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we've also had the explanation as to what each is designed to do. Having collapsed at 11.30, is it right that spontaneous circulation returned as soon as 11.36 with [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So I think -- was this the time that he only needed one dose of adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. One of the things which was -- again, I don't have my statement in front of me, but I recall -- was it at this time that it says he was very vigorous and breathing against the ventilator, so he was given some morphine --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: -- which again is -- so when you have a baby who is sick, who has sort of gone downhill and gradually become unwell to the point that you have intubated and ventilated them, they don't bounce back that quickly that in 5 minutes they'll be wanting to get this tube out, "I don't want this anymore". So that's basically the baby complaining that they don't like the tube down their throat, which is why we've gone and given him some morphine to sedate him.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Can we break that down? 11.30, collapse requiring -- again, was there --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you for saying that. To such an extent that he required the full resuscitation programme, if we put it that way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Those drugs that you have told us about, the first dose is being administered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Six minutes later, you have spontaneous circulation again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And how soon after is the baby effectively complaining about the intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Around the same time. So what I have noted in my statement is that [Baby P] fighting the ventilator and breathing against the ventilator. When babies are being ventilated artificially with an endotracheal tube and we are giving them artificial ventilation, it's not ideal that they should be breathing against the ventilator, so we then have to take measures to try
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: and stop them breathing or synchronise with the ventilator somehow.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you were, and I'm sorry for interrupting, telling us that it came as a surprise that he displayed that behaviour --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- so quickly afterwards?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just explain to us why that was such a surprise, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Because basically, if a baby -- the first collapse was unusual. There was no reason for him to have suddenly dropped his oxygen levels and his heart rate. There had been nothing to suggest that. We had taken the necessary measures and resuscitated him and were still trying to work out what had actually happened, which was -- when you're thinking, "I don't get what is going on here, I need to discuss this with someone", and that someone at that moment in time is a tertiary specialist, which is why I'd gone and spoken to Dr Rackham, you're asking yourself, okay, I've done ABC, the baby is now stable, I don't understand what's going on, I need to speak to someone else and use their expertise, to include their advice in this.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's all going on and then while -- there's no reason again for him to collapse a second time, but it happens, and then he comes back very quickly and not only does he start breathing again, he's very vigorous, he's breathing against, he's kicking and he's complaining, which means that whatever event happened was a short period and then his circulation was back and he was --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a very rapid recovery from a very low point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How did [Baby P] appear in that period then when he was resisting the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So he was -- what babies then do is you see them moving their arms and legs and they're trying to breathe and gag. And they open their mouths and you can see that they are appearing distressed from the intervention that...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How would you have described -- it's a snapshot, I suppose, but how would you have described generally [Baby P]'s condition at that moment in time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: At that moment in time I would have thought, well, okay, he's come back quite quickly -- and I think one of the things is you -- what you do is very mechanical in that time, you deal with each situation as it's happening and you're trying to count -- because the only thing in your mind at that point is, how do I make this baby better, what do I do, and what do I have to do? So when a baby collapses, you give them adrenaline, you do CPR, you do the intubation, you've done that. Then if it happens again, you do the same thing again. So you're countering or trying to deal with every problem as it happens.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at this point in time I see a baby who's come back very quickly, who's vigorous, but he's not -- I'm not in a place to say, well, okay, you're vigorous, you don't like your tube, I'm going to take the tube out.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't do that, I have to leave that tube in because this baby is having these collapses that I don't understand. So I then have to find a way to try and sedate him so he doesn't fight the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. I think the medication that was given to [Baby P] at that stage was pancuronium; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Did he not have morphine before that? Because I think at one point he had 100 micrograms per kilogram of morphine first and then he had the pancuronium.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did that have the desired effect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. With the pancuronium, what the pancuronium does is it just stops them moving, it paralyses you. Basically it's a drug that paralyses you. That means that you can control the baby's breathing completely. They do not move, you breathe for them, you basically have to make sure that the ventilation settings are optimal and you can anticipate that the baby is not putting in any effort, but that also means that you have control over their breathing and by ventilation you can't cause any harm.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. What I would like you to look at next, please, if we can go back to tile 178, you comment on a blood gas record that was taken not too long after this episode at 12.08.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can scroll down, please, I'm going to ask you to look at the penultimate entry on that particular line.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The 12.03 gas, this -- I remember being very pleased with this gas when I saw it because this had come after a few very poor gases. There's one that's not here which was a 6-pointsomething as well which is in my statement and it's in another gas record but that's not been entered here.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the 12.03 gas, the pH of 7.32, which is very good. A CO2 of 3.33, which is low normal, which means we are ventilating him well. A PO2 of 5.72 is the capillary gas; that doesn't worry me. Base excess is minus 11.4, which is quite high, and this was a problem that we, as you can see from the previous gases as well, that's been progressively rising so this is metabolic acidosis, which means that the tissues are being deprived of oxygen, and that is producing the lactate which -- despite us having given him quite a few doses of bicarbonate and he went onto a bicarbonate infusion as well later on. That is minus 11.4, but to me that was -- I remember breathing a sigh of relief, phew, because by this time I'd spoken to Dr Rackham a few times, they were on their way and I am thinking, okay, we've paralysed him, we've got control of his ventilation, we've done a gas, the gas is good, so yes, we are dealing with the metabolic acidosis and, fine, the transport team are going to be here soon, we're going to be okay. I just remember that sort of sigh of relief at that point.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Bearing in mind in his recent intubation, what does that gas, if anything, tell you about the effectiveness or otherwise of his ventilation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That it is effective, that his ventilation is working.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he has been paralysed now, we have sort of dealt with the fact that he was fighting the ventilator. We don't know why it's happened still. We are just, as I said, trying to deal with the problems as we are facing them, not quite understanding why these collapses have happened. But where we are from his airway/breathing point of view, I am reasonably satisfied, circulation I'm not very happy with, with the base excess of minus 11.4, but I feel like we're getting there, things are getting better and under control.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Had you carried out any cold light tests during the course of the two resuscitations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, we had, and the cold light hadn't indicated that there might be a pneumothorax or an air leak.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But I think that changed with an X-ray taken at 11.57; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Go to tile 400, please. We can see there the time and date on the X-ray. I suspect the clue is in the question. What can you see there, on that particular X-ray?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Particularly in that chest X-ray we can see a right-sided pneumothorax, but it's not a tension pneumothorax. So the baby is intubated, I can see an endotracheal tube, I can see that there is a rim of air on the right side, you can see the lung margins, and you can see the air.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: However -- so pneumothorax is an air leak. Sometimes in babies who are otherwise not unwell, we can see small air leaks, but if the -- so a tension pneumothorax is when you get a large amount of air on one side and it pushes the heart to the other side. That is an acute emergency that you have to do something about.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that the case here?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No. So this was not a tension pneumothorax, there was no mediastinal shift, which is why at the time, given with what had happened, we decided not to do anything.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There was no mediastinal shift, there was an air leak, but that changed with the next collapse because when we move on, when he deteriorated again, one of the first things we thought about was: well, yes, it wasn't a tension pneumothorax then, but has it become one now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We needed to deal with that, so we then went on to do a needle aspiration to relieve that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In [Dr A]'s note that third deterioration took place at 12.28?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, in the timeline, does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, it does. I do remember exactly what had happened at that time as well. So with that gas that we looked at, we were sort of -- [Dr A] and I, I think, both breathed a sigh of relief. We were in nursery 2. It's an L-shaped corridor, [Dr A] and I walked down to the kitchen -- there's a little kitchen just as you enter the neonatal unit -- to make a drink. And I remember putting the kettle on and [Dr A] and I were talking
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: through -- when you are just trying to get your head round what's actually happened, talking out loud, thinking out loud.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think we got very far. So literally, I don't think the kettle had even boiled, where somebody shouted from the end of the corridor, "Can you please come now", so both of us were out of the room when that collapse happened.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was there anyone left in the room when you went out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. As far as I can remember, Staff Nurse Lucy Letby was there with him all of that time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Anyone else there when you left him?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember who called you back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No, I don't even know if I saw the person because I think we were in the kitchen and somebody just shouted -- because it was literally shouting distance, so they would have gone to the end of the corridor and shouted us because they knew where we were and we just came running back.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When you came running back, what did you find?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So as far as I can remember, he was desaturating and his heart rate was dropping and his oxygen levels were dropping as well. And it looked like this child who had been paralysed with pancuronium had dislodged his ET tube. And one of the problems with pancuronium is whilst it's very good in controlling the ventilation, the baby can't do anything for themselves, so if the tube becomes dislodged for any reason -- and it is unlikely, unless -- because the baby is not moving, they are not breathing so unless something really untoward happens, you wouldn't expect that tube to dislodge, which was why I think we had sort of walked away from it, thinking, well, you know, he's now not going to breathe or fight the vent, we have a few minutes to think about is there anything we are missing or, you know, what we need to think about.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we came back to find him crashing, that's the term you would use, and when we checked, the tube had dislodged.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you happen to recall who was in the room when you went back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I don't have a vivid memory but I do remember Lucy was at the bedside of the baby. She would have obviously asked somebody to call us.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Were you given any explanation as to what had happened when you got back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: To be honest with you, I don't remember asking for one.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That wasn't my priority at the time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What was it that caused you to believe that the problem was the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So the baby's connected to the ventilator, you are giving them breathing through the ventilator. If their oxygen levels start to drop, then the first thing you think about is, is the ventilator and the tube doing what they're meant to be doing? Because in a paralysed baby, it's the tube and the ventilator doing everything, the baby can't do anything. So you're basically -- literally one of the things -- first things you think about -- and if you're not supplied with oxygen through the ventilator for long enough, it's only a matter of time before your heart gets deprived of oxygen as well and starts dropping as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the first thing you go to in a baby who's paralysed and starts to drop their saturations is, "Is there a problem with the tube?"
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Did you examine the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I must have had a listen, tried to bag and checked if either there was no air entry or the chest wasn't inflating, but that decision was probably made quite quickly that the tube wasn't in anymore. Yes, I think I've written the capnograph wasn't changing colour.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's one way of finding out.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What happened then to the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: We removed that tube and [Dr A] re-intubated him.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: For a third time, was cardiopulmonary resuscitation recommenced?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What happened this time? Can you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: This time, as well, he received multiple doses of adrenaline, sodium chloride, sodium bicarbonate. We also commenced him on adrenaline infusion. I think this was -- around
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: this time, 12.20, was around the time to, give him a constant supply of -- either at this time or maybe a bit later on he went on two more infusions of dopamine and dobutamine to, again, improve his circulation and his cardiac contractility.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Were any measures taken regarding, at this stage, the pneumothorax that you'd seen about --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. Again, with the -- you'll have to go back to the statement to consult with the time. So one of first things we then also thought about with this collapse once the ventilation had happened was to needle the pneumothorax, the right side. The needling of the pneumothorax is that you insert a cannula and allow the air to come out. So that's an emergency procedure, which always should be followed by inserting a chest drain. However, a chest drain insertion is an aseptic and a fairly sort of lengthy procedure. It's not a -- in an emergency, it's a procedure we call needle thoracocentesis. So you put a needle in and you allow the air to escape. So if there is a tension pneumothorax that's causing a massive compromise, it will release the air and allow the lung to expand and then you go back and insert a chest drain properly, which is what was done.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In the context of what was happening around this time, we've mentioned 12.28, do you remember at what stage that needle was introduced to, as it were, first aid the pneumothorax --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Um...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- or would you be reliant on [Dr A]'s note for that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I would be reliant on my statement and his notes because we both did them in conjunction -- at the time when this was happening everything was happening in quick succession so thinking --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Who inserted the needle?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: [Dr A]. So basically, the first thing to do would have been to secure the airway. Needle thoracocentesis wouldn't have been a primary procedure. So you intubate the baby again, a baby who's paralysed is not breathing, you -- you tube them again and then the first thing you do is a needle thoracocentesis to release the air and then go from there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm going to ask Mr Murphy, please, to go, I think, I hope I'm right, to tile 435, please. This is [Dr A]'s note on this point. I'm going to ask you to have a look at this, please. You can see at the top the reference to the re-intubation that you told us about.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's just that second paragraph down, please, beginning "Chest X-ray".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does that suggest a chest X-ray was taken -- is that at around 12.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall that taking place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. That would have all been happening in that time, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm sorry, it's not your writing, but are you able to read what --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that "right-sided lateral" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: "Right-sided lateral pneumothorax decompressed with 24gauge Jelco at second to third intercostal space/mid-clavicular line at 12.40."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it says "2 to 3", but you might have to ask.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just dealing then with that paragraph, doctor, we've looked at the X-ray that was taken at 11.57.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Mm.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You tell us that you recall that chest X-ray being taken around 12.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No, I don't. The timeline, I am not going to be precise about. The timeline of the X-ray machine is the most accurate one because it records the time when the chest X-ray is taken. Yes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Or should do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Which... It should do, yes. Whatever time we have here, I have or [Dr A] has approximate times because these are -- we have gone back and thought about, okay, we would have done this around this time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Well, I'm going to go back to your note now, please, at 625. We can scroll to the point that we'd reached in your note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We had got, I think, to the bottom of the page, certainly on to the next page. You'd spoken to Dr Rackham, you told us, around 10.30, but on a number of occasions; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, I did. I haven't documented them all but I spoke to him a few times.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall the resolution of the resuscitation that began at around 12.28 that we've been discussing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Do I recall the resolution as in return of spontaneous circulation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. How long, from recollection, do you recall that taking?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I think it lasted several minutes and he probably needed a good few doses of adrenaline from what I can remember.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's a third resuscitation during the course of about 4 hours?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Moving on then in the timeline, if we may, and returning to your note:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Spoke to Dr Rackham."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that about 1 pm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Updated about frequent collapses with desats and bradys on ventilation and possibly pulmonary hypertensive episodes."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just explain to us a pulmonary hypertensive episode, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I was discussing with Dr Rackham -- so when I spoke to him at 1, this would have been -- did you say the fourth or the third?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The third was at 12.28.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. He must have recovered from this and by this time I was obviously becoming extremely worried and again revisiting, are we missing something here, is there something else we can do, and I spoke to Dr Rackham again. Pulmonary hypertension is a condition where -- which babies can develop in which you can intermittently have periods where lung pressures go very high and oxygenation is compromised. So we are thinking here of every box that we can that might explain why these collapses are happening. And one of the possibilities Dr Rackham suggested was -- "Is he going into pulmonary hypertensive crisis?" was one differential. And he suggested to try and get an echocardiogram to see if that's the case.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. That will be the way, would it, to determine whether that was the problem or not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you succeed in getting an echocardiogram?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. I spoke to Dr Brearey, he is one of our colleagues who has a specialist interest in cardiology, to come and do an echocardiogram. Dr Brearey did and excluded pulmonary hypertension and, basically, I think I have written he had mild tricuspid regurgitation, which is nothing to be concerned about.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Let's pause there. You're quite right to say that's the rest of your note and I just wanted to deal with that first. You've then put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Already on dopamine and adrenaline infusions"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Sorry, where are we now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After you have said --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, "Already on dopamine and adrenaline infusions".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Due to frequent deterioration..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that dobutamine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, "dobutamine prepared". So all these drugs augment each other and do slightly different things. So dopamine is good
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: for children who have poor peripheral circulation. So he had already been on that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Adrenaline, because it improves cardiac contractility and again maintains blood pressure and improves perfusion. So he was already on that. And then again, he obviously went on and had another collapse despite being on this. So one of the things Dr Rackham suggested was to add in dobutamine, which again has a special effect in improving heart contractility because we were having frequent episodes of his heart rate going down as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he was -- yes, he said, start him on dobutamine as well and get an echo done to see what is going on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you put here:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Brearey performed an echo that showed mild tricuspid regurgitation."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Anything to worry about with that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And, "Good cardiac contractility", is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, the heart -- he could see that the heart was contracting well, so obviously at the time when Dr Brearey did the echo his heart rate was good and, from what he could see, there was no reason for a pulmonary hypertensive crisis to be causing this problem.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have then put -- is that, "Continue on dobutamine"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: HCO3, that's bicarbonate, is it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Infusion..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: "... commenced over 6 hours. Full correction as per advice from Dr Rackham."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So looking at his blood gas pattern one of the things that we could see was that we gave him multiple doses of -- so normally, there is a formula we calculate of how much bicarbonate a baby needs so when you get the full -- from the formula when you get
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: the full dose, you halve it and give it over half an hour and that's it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he'd had quite a few doses of that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was collapsing repeatedly and every time we did a gas, the acidosis was worse. So it wasn't something we were getting on top of.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Persistent acidosis is not good for the heart because it has a negative effect on cardiac contractility. So we were trying to counter all these things and when I would have been speaking to Dr Rackham, I would have been giving him the gases and the metabolic acidosis worsening.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So another thing that he suggested was put him up on a continuous infusion of full correction over 6 hours, which is what he is on now.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And that's to correct that acidosis that was proving tough to shift; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Let's go on in your note, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Sorry, say that...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can go on with the note, please. Mr Murphy is just going to scroll down for us again in a moment, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your next note is about Dr Rackham, but between that phone call and 3 o'clock, I'd just likes to discuss that period with you, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After those measures suggested by Dr Rackham, how was [Baby P] up until about 3 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So between this time I think there is one gas at least.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he was relatively -- I think we also gave him in this time some metronidazole to cover for necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Rackham also asked to give him a start dose of hydrocortisone just in case there might be an element of what we call adrenal crisis. So we took a cortisol level and gave him that and again these are all the differentials going through everybody's mind.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So very sick babies, the adrenal gland produces a very important hormone, cortisol, which helps us fight stress and sickness. If a baby is not producing that in the right amount then that can be the cause of collapse, so we did that blood level and gave him some hydrocortisone. We also give him some metronidazole.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Both of these were given through the intraosseous route.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He had a gas -- I'll have to ask you to check the time -- of 7.25, which is not great, but still --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just pause there. We'll put it up for you if that helps. Everyone will have seen it, it's the last one on the sheet, sadly. It's at 13.38.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's the last venous sample entered on the record.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the one you were trying to remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. This is a pH of 7.25, which is borderline normal/okay/acceptable. His carbon dioxide levels are fine, which means that his ventilation is not an issue.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: His oxygen PO2 is fine, but his acidosis is worse. So his base excess is minus 13.8 and his lactate is 18.5, which is extremely high and worrying.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this is all metabolic now. Breathing-wise, we've got control, it's just his circulation is that poor and there is that much acidosis around that it's causing him -- his body to produce a large amount of lactate and his acidosis.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You mentioned a numbered of things. Is it also right that [Baby P] received a dose of Curosurf, surfactant --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- during the course of the afternoon as well?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And do you recall [Dr A], once it was considered appropriate, you told us you couldn't do it in an unstable baby, but did there come a point when [Dr A] felt able to do something with that temporary needle that you told us about to drain the pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, so between the time of -- after the collapse at 12.30 and re-intubation, in the period of stabilisation that followed
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Dr A] successfully sited a chest drain and there was an X-ray confirming that that pneumothorax has resolved.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. [Dr A]'s note was that that was at 3 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does that accord with your recollection as best you can remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I don't recollect the exact times, but...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Let's have a look at -- I would like you to look at two X-rays, please. If we go first to tile 434.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we actually look at the X-ray, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Unfortunately, not timed or dated, this one, doctor, hence my reservation earlier --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- but we saw [Dr A]'s note. Is this before the drain was fitted?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The drain is in situ now. So this tube that's coming in (indicating) is the drain and you can see that the pneumothorax has resolved. The endotracheal tube is in and the lungs are inflated.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. I'd like you to look at another X-ray, please, which is tile 574, which is timed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, that's a pigtail.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just comparing the two, I'm not going to go back to it, the difference there is the pigtail, is it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So that's the one that takes longer to insert and you need a field of aseptic area and it takes a good half an hour to insert. So this would have happened --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's 3.36 and would be consistent with [Dr A]'s note that it was put in at or around 3 o'clock --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Around that time, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. With apologies to Mr Murphy for skipping around, can we go back to 625, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I want to pick your note up at 3 o'clock, please, which I think is on the third page, if I remember rightly:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Rackham arrived with..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that the transport nurse, in effect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Staff nurse, SN is staff nurse.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... with transfer team at 3 pm as chest drain was being inserted and fixed."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So again, consistent with [Dr A]'s note. And then sadly:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Shortly thereafter, [Baby P] deteriorated again."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall where you were when that happened?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I was in that room, speaking to Dr Rackham, giving him -- I had spoken to him on a good few occasions during the day and I remember he was just standing opposite me and there were quite a lot of people in the room, but I don't recall who else was there. I was speaking to him and giving him handover on the events through the day --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: -- and [Baby P] started to deteriorate again, oxygen levels dropping, heart rate dropping, and full cardiac resuscitation was started again.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I hope this doesn't sound a daft question, I appreciate you were in the room, but how were you alerted to [Baby P]'s sudden deterioration?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: It would have been either the alarms going off or -because we were in the room, so it would have been pretty much in front of us.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, okay. You mentioned that the resuscitation procedure began again.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This time we've heard it went on for some considerable time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But sadly, on this occasion, it was not successful?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We heard this morning that, having arrived during the course of this, Dr Rackham took control of the situation; is that your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And beyond assisting him, did you have any other interaction with [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No. I think one of the things he added was -- we doubled the dose of adrenaline, so he had instead of 0.1ml per kilogram, 0.2ml per kilogram. Another thing Dr Rackham added was: is there a possibility that he could be having seizures, so let's give him a loading dose of phenobarbitone. So we gave him that. Another thing, because of the persistent bradycardia, adrenaline wasn't touching him, his adrenaline infusion had been doubled. We -- sorry, just one second. Yes, atropine is another drug that we don't use very commonly for resuscitations, but he just said to give him a dose of that, so we tried that as well but it didn't do anything.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It wasn't successful?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Okay. Before we move on to the remainder of your note, can I ask you this: you told us -- you've given us an idea of who was there throughout the afternoon and at particular times. Any conversations with any of those people that stick in your mind?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So one conversation that sticks in my mind is, you know that, when was it, just after the 12 o'clock gas, the 7.32 one. So we had that gas and after that -- so how we have the old neonatal unit, this was nursery 2, and then there's nursery 1, which is a bigger room. So I remember going there, to nursery 1, and there were a few nurses present there, including Staff Nurse Lucy Letby. And I remember -- so when you face one wall, there's a clock in front and I remember looking at that clock and it was going just past 12. And I just said, "Oh, the transport team are going to be here soon", almost thinking out loud more than anything else, and I'm literally sort of counting the minutes before they arrive, just desperately wanting this baby to get better and thinking, you know, there's something -- you're just totally out of your depth, can't think what's going on, maybe somebody else can come and help.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And Staff Nurse Letby says, "He's not leaving here alive, is he?" which I found absolutely shocking at the time and I just turned round and I said, "Don't say that, he's had a good gas."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I just remember that's just -- all these years on, what, 7 years on, 6 years on, that moment is still very much alive in my mind and I said this and I left the room, but found that very -because, yes, you know, we have babies -- all through our careers we see babies who are very, very sick, who are very, very unwell, and with some of them who have followed a course and have become progressively unwell, even when we know that their chances are survival are very poor, personally, for me, that's something I would never let myself think because it's that hope that makes you keep trying. So I just found that very, very -- I don't even know if I was upset, I think I was just shocked at the time, I was just shocked.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Just pausing there then, you remember the time roughly?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: It was just between 12 and quarter past because he had just had this gas, I'd had the gas and I'd come out of that room and gone to another room.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is the gas that you have described to us as being --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The 7.35 or 7.321.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The one that you were pleased with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So how would you describe [Baby P] -- albeit relative to what had been going on, but how was he at the moment that conversation took place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: At that point in time, since that morning, he was the best you could call him. We'd managed -- this was a kid that had had a good gas, he was ventilated, he was stable, the transport team were on their way, so I thought we were winning and found no reason for this comment, really.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Through the course of the afternoon any other conversations with anybody that stick in your mind?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So after [Baby P] passed away, we -- so we have through -when you go through to the labour ward, which is literally a connecting door from the neonatal unit, Lavender Suite, where the parents were. So myself and Staff Nurse Lucy Letby went down there and I went to speak to the parents.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I remember feeling -- you know, when you just feel, "I don't know how to face them, I don't know how to say this". So I went
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: there and the parents were sitting there and I told them that [Baby P] too was going to need a post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Staff Nurse Letby was behind me against the door, against a shelf, and again one of the things that I found unusual was -she was almost sort of very animated in that she was saying to the parents, "Do you want me to make you a memory box, a memory box for him, you know like I did for [Baby O] yesterday?" And I just remember thinking: this is not a new baby, this is a dead baby, why are you so excited about this?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Why do you use the word "excited"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Because that's how she was. She was just, "Do you want me to make you a memory box?" Like you make -- you know, babies upstairs get these, what do you call them, bounty packs or whatever, you know, newborns, they get this from the hospital or someone where they have different little things. And the parents were like, "Yes, please, that would be nice, thank you", and I found that very inappropriate, the way it was said.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not what was said?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No, not what was said, there was nothing wrong with the content of it, it was just how it was said.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So dealing with the period after [Baby P] had passed away, can we just conclude your note, please? If we can turn back to that, please. You've reiterated:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "For detailed notes on resus, please refer to [Dr A]'s notes. At around 4.30 [is that] spoke to Chris at the coroner's office..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Mm.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... the senior coroner's officer, Christine Hurst."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Scroll down, please, Mr Murphy. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have noted that it was agreed that both triplets' deaths -and you have quoted:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... unexplained and would require a coroner's post-mortem"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You then put the contact details for Christine Hurst and also her home number, which has been obviously taken out,
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: and that she could be contacted over the weekend if needed; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then you have noted that [Baby R] was transferred to Liverpool Women's Hospital. Anything you can recall about that process of [Baby R] being taken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So I just remember thinking at the time I remember dad was there and he was absolutely sobbing, stood next to [Baby P], and literally begging Dr Rackham, "Can you please take him?" And even though I didn't beg, I said to Dr Rackham in a more professional way, in my mind and heart I just wanted him to leave because I thought that's the only way he's going to live.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You thought that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, I thought that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And Dr Rackham agreed to take [Baby R]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, he was very good about that, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then you put that you spoke to them, the parents, about the post-mortem, sadly a conversation that you had already had on 23 June after [Baby O]'s death?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And they wished for [Baby O] and [Baby P] to be transferred to the mortuary for the weekend:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I informed them, as per discussion with the coroner's office, that both triplets would be transferred to..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that Arrowe --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... Alder Hey on Monday when various specimens for testing for infection, genetic and metabolic conditions would be taken and they would be returned to the parents by the end of next week for funeral arrangements."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then you carry on with the arrangements for more time with [Baby O] and [Baby P] if they wished. Perhaps we don't need to — if we scroll down a bit more. You gave dad your secretary's number so you could be contacted if necessary and also for the
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: parents to call if they had any questions and you'd arranged to meet them.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That, I think, concludes your note with your signature, doctor; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. I have no more questions, but I don't know whether that's...
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. We'll have a break. Can we start again at 20 to, so in about 8 minutes? Will that be sufficient time for you? I'm anxious that this witness completes her evidence this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
I don't know how long you'll be, Mr Myers, but I don't think it would be appropriate to start another witness this afternoon, Mr Driver.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, I think not, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: [Dr B], we have a sort of eight-minute or so break now. Do you wish to leave the court room for any purpose or are you happy to remain there?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR B: Could I go to the toilet?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR B: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When this was ongoing, you've told us about an exchange between you and Nurse Letby, things that were, you say, said by her or something that was said by her. Do you remember telling us about that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you've said she' said, "He's not leaving here alive, is he"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: First of all, is that the precise words or is that casting your mind back at the time you were asked to recall this, something along those lines?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: As far as I remember, that was how it was.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you recall telling the police it was a comment along the lines of, "He's not leaving here alive, is he"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, along those lines. Now, as it happens, he had been struggling, hadn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He'd had to be given resuscitation on one or more occasions by this point, hadn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And he'd had to be given adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, for which we couldn't understand the whats and whys of.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you were very concerned as to whether or not he'd be stable enough to make it on to the transport, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: At that point, no.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, you've told us that after the first -- after four collapses and -- at least four collapses and three to four doses of adrenaline, this was --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: No, he'd only had two by this time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But you were concerned about events the day before with [Baby O], weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: At that point in time, as I've said before, I was not thinking about [Baby O]. So as this day was progressing, my mind was miles away from what had happened the day before because you can't focus on a sick kid, managing what you're managing, trying to think, and likening it to anything that had happened the day before. At that point in time, my focus was: this kid has gone off out of nowhere; we've brought him back once; then he's gone briefly the second time; he's come back again; I don't know what's going on with him; he's stable at the minute; I'm hoping we can get him out and get him better. That's where I was.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At the time of this comment you were worried, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, of course I was worried, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And in fact, you've said to us, just as you were leading up to what you say Nurse Letby said, you said it went like this. You said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The transport team are going to be here soon. I was desperately wanting the baby to get better."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Feeling totally out of your depth, wanting someone else to come. Those were your words.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Feeling totally out of your depth?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, because I didn't know what had prompted and caused those collapses in a baby who at 9.30 was reasonably stable and
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: went on and had a cardiac arrest 10 minutes later. That's just not something I have seen in the 17 years of my consultant career.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you were concerned?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, I was concerned.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And maybe all she was doing was making it plain that she's concerned?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: I can only speak for myself.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But it's simply expressing a concern that actually isn't that different from your concern, [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: I can only tell you my perception of how I perceived the comments.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you think there's a danger here, because it's Lucy Letby we're dealing with, things she's said or done being taken out of context and being made to sound quite a lot worse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: I found it highly unusual, given the circumstances and the fact that we are in these situations in different times of having really sick babies and kids, but making such comments is not something we do.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You may have regarded it, however it was said, as an inappropriate comment.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. That's my personal opinion.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. But you agree at this point, certainly in your mind was a real anxiety of what was going to happen to [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. When it comes to Nurse Letby assisting with the memory box and events towards the conclusion of this, [Dr B], it had been an incredibly distressing day so far as you could tell for everyone involved in it, hadn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And it fell to Nurse Letby to assist the family with what happened after a bereavement had happened because she was the designated nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You've described how she seemed to be, I think you put it, excited, "Do you want me to make a memory box?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Shall I do this for you? Shall I do that for you?"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's how --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: "Shall I do it the same way like I did for [Baby O] yesterday?"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, all right. Not the way you would have gone about it if you were in that position; is that what you're suggesting?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But entirely possible she's going about it in an upbeat way, which, trying to be upbeat, you regard as inappropriate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When you say "excited", that could be something she's doing just to try and sound better than it actually is?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's a good deal of criticism directed towards Ms Letby, directly or indirectly. I want to give you the opportunity to comment on some evidence that we have had, [Dr B]. All right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: During the course of looking after [Baby P], did you have any kind of infection yourself? Were you coughing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Were you spluttering? You smile, you know what I might be raising.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's comments from the statement of [Mother of Babies O & P].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You know the passage I'm referring to perhaps:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Dr B] was coughing and spluttering and going out for a smoke and never washing her hands."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: I think that happened once. It wasn't more than once as far as I remember. Yes, it did happen once and it's not something I'm proud of. No, I did not have an infection. I wasn't unwell at the time. I did cough, I had gone out for a cigarette, came back, didn't wash my hands. I don't remember doing it, but I must have coughed and then gone to the child again, so yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All of which are particular things she may have focused upon, but you would say that hardly sums up the whole degree of your effort to help [Baby P], does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, absolutely. But they were very right in observing that and it was wrong of me to do what I did.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. But it's entirely possible to pick on little things like that -- I'm not being difficult with [Mother of Babies O & P] when I say that -- but pick on one or two items. But the reality is, in fact, your efforts were directing at looking after [Baby P], weren't they? And in fact, all those people dealing with [Baby P], from what you could see in the course of this, were all doing their best to look after him, from what you could see?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And that goes for Nurse Letby, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you, my Lord, I'm grateful we could sit late.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR B: Thank you. Thank you, everyone.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, there is nothing in re-examination, thank you, unless my Lord has anything.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much, [Dr B]. Stay there. Will [Dr B] be required again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Possibly. I'm sorry to put it so opaquely.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It doesn't matter. In those circumstances, please don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right? You'll obviously be notified as and when if you are required.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right, members of the jury, thank you very much indeed today for going the extra 12 minutes. 10.30 tomorrow morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
It is very warm in here, Mr Myers, and it feels very airless as well.
It often seems to strike at this point in the day as well, which is where I'm often located.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It is uncomfortably hot, even for people who like it warm.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can I apologise for the alarm, deliberately set after 4.30?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not a problem, Mr Astbury. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mr Myers, will someone...?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The timing is a little too tight this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No one will be able to come down and see Ms Letby now. Thank you very much. So your transport arrangements can go ahead, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm sorry if I caused confusion about the possibility of another witness. I had anticipated we would be the rest or most of the rest of the afternoon with [Dr B]. It's just the earlier comment from Mr Driver that I was becoming rather confused by.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Crossed wires, my Lord, but there was no difficulty created by that. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Please remain where you are, [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed. I will rise. Everyone else will leave the court and then you'll be escorted from the courtroom.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Wednesday, 22 March 2023)
